title: Beha'alotcha: a second Passover (Numbers 9:6–14)
hook: people who missed Passover ask for a chance, and one is given

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aaron held the light until it rose alone, and your line was until it rises alone. Did you stay with someone through a first try, then step back? Day four hundred forty-two.

A group of people walk up to Moses with a complaint that sounds almost like a lawsuit. Everyone else is getting ready to keep Passover in the wilderness, a year after leaving Egypt. The lambs are chosen. The fires are being built. And these people can't take part. It's not their fault. They're ritually impure, because they've been near a dead body. Somebody had to handle the dead. And they want to know: why should we be left out? What happens next is striking. Moses doesn't give them an answer. He says: wait, and I'll ask.
screen: `EVERYONE IS READY FOR PASSOVER.` → `A GROUP LEFT OUT.` → `MOSES SAYS: WAIT.`

segments.voice: Numbers nine. The men say: we're impure from a dead body, "wherefore are we to be kept back," from bringing the LORD's offering at its time with everyone else? Moses tells them to wait while he asks. This law doesn't start as a command from above. It starts from below: it starts with people who refuse to accept being shut out, and say so. God's answer creates a new date. Anyone impure from the dead, or far away on a journey, can keep Passover one month later, on the fourteenth of the second month, with matzah and bitter herbs. In Hebrew, Pesach Sheni: the second Passover. Who were they? The Talmud records a few opinions. One says they were the people carrying Joseph's coffin, the bones Moses brought out of Egypt. Another suggests they had buried someone who died with no one else to bury them. Either way, they were impure because they'd done something good. The Torah is honest about the edge of this, too. For someone who was clean, not on a journey, and simply didn't keep Passover, the verse has hard words: he shall bear his sin. The second date is written for people life got in the way of. Today, there's no Passover offering, but the date is still marked. Some Jews eat a piece of matzah on that day, a month after Passover. And in Chabad teaching it's often summed up with a simple line: it's never too late. The door you missed can open again.
screen: `WHEREFORE ARE WE KEPT BACK?` · `A LAW THAT STARTS FROM BELOW.` · `ONE MONTH LATER: PESACH SHENI.` · `FOR THOSE LIFE GOT IN THE WAY OF.` · then, large: `SECOND CHANCES EXIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone a second chance. Breathe, and think of someone who missed something with you: a birthday, a promise, a deadline, a moment you needed them. Ask whether life got in the way of them, the way it did for the people in the story. Hold that possibility gently. Then picture offering a second date: let's try again next week, I'd still like to hear about it, the door's open. You can also offer yourself one. The bell holds the time.
Pesach Sheni. The second Passover: one month later, for those who couldn't keep the first, given because they asked.
Your line: second chances exist. Today, offer one, to someone else or to yourself, with a real date on it. Day four hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Pesach Sheni falls on the fourteenth of Iyar, a month after Passover; with no Temple offering today, some Jews mark it by eating some matzah, and some communities omit penitential prayers that day.

fork.setup: you're Moses. men who couldn't keep Passover ask why they should be left out. what do you do?
options: tell them the rules are the rules.
tell them to wait while you ask God.
fork.reveal: Moses doesn't answer on the spot; he tells them to wait. God answers with a whole new date: Pesach Sheni, a month later.

original.note: Hebrew: the second Passover. sheni means second.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you miss a holy day, it's simply gone.
what it means: the Torah gave those who missed Passover through no fault of their own a second date.
what a scholar hears: Sukkah 25a offers views that the men carried Joseph's coffin, or had buried an abandoned corpse.

notes: 'wherefore are we to be kept back' from JPS 1917 Numbers 9:7, from memory; confirm.
Sukkah 25a–b: views that the men carried Joseph's coffin (Rabbi Yose HaGelili), were Mishael and Elzaphan (Rabbi Akiva), or had buried a met mitzvah (Rabbi Yitzchak). The script names two; confirm.

Review pass: 'it's never too late' was attributed to 'the last Lubavitcher Rebbe'. The line appears in Hayom Yom (14 Iyar) in the name of the sixth Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, and was later taught widely by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson; 'last' is also a sensitive word for some Chabad followers. Now phrased as 'in Chabad teaching'. Confirm.
Customs (eating matzah, omitting Tachanun) vary and are most common in Hasidic and some Sephardi communities; review pass softened 'many' to 'some'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'the first Passover since leaving Egypt' replaced with what Numbers 9:1 says (the second year); cut 'unusual in the Torah' and 'most of the Torah's laws come down from above'; 'Moses doesn't know' now matches 9:8 (he tells them to wait); the claim that someone who skipped by choice 'isn't given the same chance' was stronger than the text and contested in the Talmud (Pesachim 93a), so the teach and myth now say only what 9:13 says.
